report:
**Conclusion: yes—probably, particularly when a community program gets many people to wear well-fitting medical/surgical masks consistently.** The best direct evidence is a large cluster-randomized trial in 600 Bangladeshi villages (342,183 adults). Mask promotion raised observed use from about 13% to 42% and reduced *symptomatic, test-confirmed* SARS‑CoV‑2 infection by 9.3% overall. The benefit was clearer for surgical than cloth masks and larger among older adults. Because entire villages—not merely individuals—were assigned, this is strong evidence for a population-level effect, including source control (infected people reducing virus emitted) and wearer protection.  
https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abi9069  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34855513/

The conclusion should not be overstated. The trial tested a bundle—free masks, education, reminders, and community enforcement—in rural Bangladesh during 2020–21, so the exact effect will vary with mask type/fit, uptake, ventilation, crowding, immunity, and circulating variant. An individual wearing a mask in a mostly unmasked setting is not the same intervention as high community use.

Why is the evidence sometimes described as uncertain? A Cochrane review of randomized trials across respiratory viruses found uncertainty about masks’ average effect, largely because studies differed greatly and often had low adherence, indirect outcomes, or methodological limitations. That does **not** establish that masks do not work; it means many trials were poorly positioned to measure the real-world effect of widespread, consistent use.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD006207_do-physical-measures-such-hand-washing-or-wearing-masks-stop-or-slow-down-spread-respiratory-viruses
